A close reading for the week

“the print of a man’s naked foot”

Robinson Crusoe · the footprint

After some fifteen years alone, the castaway who has prayed for human company finds evidence of it: a single footprint on his shore. What follows is a close study of fear changing everything he sees.

It happened one day, about noon,1 going towards my boat, I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man’s naked foot on the shore,2 which was very plain to be seen on the sand.

  1. 1

    Noon, going to the boat

    The sentence opens like an entry in an account-book: one day, about noon, on the way to the boat. Defoe’s realism works by this flatness: the most shattering event in the novel is time-stamped like a delivery. The style has spent two hundred pages recording goats, crops and gunpowder in this same voice, which is why the interruption lands so hard. The ledger was not built for apparitions.

  2. 2

    One print, naked, singular

    Each word counts. A “print” is evidence of a person without the person: a human being reduced to a sign. “Naked” says the foot was unshod, and Crusoe soon decides it belongs to one of the people he calls savages, and not to a European sailor; the fear has a colonial shape almost from the start. And it is singular: one print, with no track leading to or from it. Whether or not Defoe planned that impossibility, the strangeness adds to the fear.
